sections.h2: Who has the legal right to sell a house after an Oregon owner dies?
sections.html:
Usually the court-appointed personal representative, not an heir or a person named in the will. Under ORS 114.215, title to a dead person's property passes to the heirs or devisees, but it stays subject to administration and sale by the personal representative. That representative takes possession and control of the estate under ORS 114.225.

The Oregon Real Estate Agency tells brokers the same thing in plain terms. Being named in a will or being an heir does not by itself give someone the right to sell. The agency lists warning signs that should stop a deal: probate not filed, a very recent death, someone calling themselves executor without going through the court, several heirs, and no attorney involved.

For a family, the practical result is simple. Before any buyer can close, someone has to hold court papers showing an appointment, or the estate has to qualify for a shortened procedure.

sections.h2: How does a personal representative get appointed in Oregon?
sections.html:
An interested person or the person nominated in the will files a petition with the circuit court. ORS 113.035 says the petition must list the heirs and devisees and estimate the extent of the assets.

When more than one person wants the job, ORS 113.085 sets the order of preference:

  • The personal representative named in the will
  • The surviving spouse
  • Intestate heirs who receive a share
  • Other people who receive a share
  • The director of the state human services or health agency, or an approved attorney
  • The Department of Veterans' Affairs, then anyone else

If a person dies with no will and no known heirs, the State Treasurer is appointed, and ORS 113.238 requires notice to the Treasurer within 48 hours of learning of such a death. The court sets any bond based on the estate's assets, income and debts (ORS 113.105). Marion County's court describes the general path: petition, appointment, collection of assets, payment of debts, an accounting to the court, and distribution.

sections.h2: Can a personal representative sell the house without asking the judge?
sections.html:
In most estates, yes. ORS 114.325 gives the representative power to sell, mortgage or lease estate property without notice, a hearing or a court order.

There are two catches. A sale needs notice, a hearing and an order if it would go against the terms of the will. The same is true if the house was specifically left to someone and the will does not authorize a sale. If the representative will not act, ORS 114.335 lets an interested person ask the court to order a sale.

A few rules protect the person on the other side of the table:

  • A buyer who deals with the representative without actual knowledge of an improper act is protected as if the power were properly used (ORS 114.385).
  • The buyer does not have to track how the sale money is later spent.
  • Property sold by a representative stays subject to liens against the decedent or the estate, but not to creditor claims against the heirs (ORS 114.345).
  • A sale to the representative or to certain related parties is voidable unless an exception applies (ORS 114.355).

sections.h2: What is the probate timeline for an Oregon house sale?
sections.html:
Expect several months at minimum. Marion County's court says probate takes at least four months, that most cases close in under a year, and that the average runs six to nine months.

The statutes build that schedule from a handful of fixed clocks.

StepDeadlineStatute
Information to heirs and deviseesWithin 30 days of appointmentORS 113.145
Search for creditors3 months after appointment, unless the court allows longerORS 115.003
Notice to known claimantsWithin 30 days after the search period endsORS 115.003
Claims barred if not presentedLater of 4 months after published notice or 45 days after a mailed noticeORS 115.005
Will contest4 months after the heirs information is delivered or mailedORS 113.075
Supplemental inventory for later-found propertyWithin 30 days of learning of itORS 113.175
Notice of final account and distributionMailed at least 20 days before the objection dateORS 116.093

A sale can usually close before the estate is fully wrapped up, because the representative already holds the power to sell. The proceeds then sit with the estate until the court approves distribution.

sections.h2: What does probate cost, and how is the personal representative paid?
sections.html:
The main costs are the filing fee, the cost of publishing notice, bond if one is required, attorney fees, and the representative's fee. Marion County's court also lists accountants, appraisers, repairs and sale costs as common extras.

The representative's commission comes from a sliding scale in ORS 116.173:

  • 7 percent of the first $1,000
  • 4 percent of the amount from $1,000 up to $10,000
  • 3 percent of the amount from $10,000 up to $50,000
  • 2 percent of anything above $50,000

Marion County's page gives $4,630 as the statutory fee on a $200,000 estate, and that matches the scale above. The fee can be waived, and the court may allow extra pay for unusual work. The representative also needs court approval before paying representative or attorney fees or handing property to heirs.

Because the percentages apply to the property the court supervises, a house that sells for a high price raises the fee. Heirs weighing a quick sale against a long listing should ask the estate attorney to run both numbers.

sections.h2: How do creditors and unpaid bills affect the sale of an inherited house?
sections.html:
Creditors have to present claims to the personal representative, and filing a claim with the court does not count. ORS 115.005 bars a claim that is not presented in time, and ORS 115.025 requires it in writing with the amount, if known, and the claimant's name and address.

When the estate cannot pay everyone, ORS 115.125 sets a ranking. Support obligations and costs of administration come first. Wages earned in the 90 days before death rank higher than general creditors, and all other claims land at the bottom, paid in proportion within their class.

Liens on the house itself are a separate matter. Under ORS 114.345 a sale by the representative does not wipe out liens that attached to the decedent's property. They are usually paid from the sale money at closing, which is one reason heirs ask for a payoff statement early.

sections.h2: What if the estate has no personal representative yet and the house is vacant?
sections.html:
The family has two options: start probate or check whether a shortened procedure fits the estate. Neither can be skipped by simply signing a purchase contract. The agency's guidance to brokers is to pause and send the person to an attorney when there is no court paperwork.

Once a representative is appointed, ORS 114.265 tells the representative to settle the estate as promptly as is reasonable and with as little loss of value as possible. In practice that is a strong reason to decide early whether to repair and list the house or sell it as is.

sections.h2: Does probate look different from county to county in Oregon?
sections.html:
The statutes are the same statewide, but each court posts its own forms, hours and local practice. Oregon has 36 counties, from Multnomah at the top of the population list to Wheeler at the bottom.

Marion County's court page is a good example of what a county circuit court publishes: forms, a fee schedule reference, and a plain summary of what the representative must do. It also points to ways property can pass outside court, such as jointly owned accounts with survivorship and payable-on-death accounts.

Heirs who live out of state still need the same court appointment before a buyer can close, so asking the local court clerk for its forms is a sensible first call.

sections.h2: How are the final account and distribution handled after the house sells?
sections.html:
The representative files an account and asks the court to approve distribution. ORS 116.083 requires the account to cover the period, money and property received, payments made and property on hand, with a declaration under penalty of perjury.

The final account adds statements that required estate tax returns and Oregon taxes are filed or paid, a statement of the representative's pay, and a petition for a judgment of distribution. If all distributees consent in writing and every creditor is paid in full, a simpler statement can replace the full account.

Marion County's court notes the representative must keep estate money in a separate account in the representative's name, so closing proceeds go there.

faqs.q: Can I sell my parent's house in Oregon if I am the only child but there is no will?
faqs.a: Not on your own signature until you have authority. Being the only heir does not by itself let you sign a sale. The usual route is to petition for appointment as personal representative, and ORS 113.085 puts surviving heirs high in the order of preference after a spouse. A small estate may qualify for a shorter procedure, so ask an attorney which path fits.

faqs.q: Does the court have to approve the sale price of an inherited Oregon house?
faqs.a: Usually not. ORS 114.325 lets a personal representative sell without a hearing or court order. A court order is needed if the sale would go against the will, or if the house was specifically left to someone and the will gives no power to sell.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to make claims against the estate?
faqs.a: Four months after the published notice, or 45 days after a mailed notice, whichever is later. The claim has to be presented to the personal representative, not just filed with the court (ORS 115.005).

faqs.q: What does the Oregon Real Estate Agency say about listing a house after an owner dies?
faqs.a: It tells brokers to confirm legal authority before signing a listing agreement. If probate has not been filed, there are several heirs, or the person has no attorney, the agency says to pause and recommend counsel.

faqs.q: Who gets the money if the house sells during probate?
faqs.a: The estate does. The proceeds go into the estate account, and the court must approve fees and any distribution to heirs. What is left after debts, taxes and costs goes to the heirs or devisees under the will or Oregon intestacy law.
